idiom_name: BlockingQueue<Order> (java.util.concurrent) or a JMS queue/topic per message type
implementation_notes: For in-process hand-off java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue<E> is the typed channel: a LinkedBlockingQueue<Order> with put()/take() gives blocking transfer plus an optional capacity bound, and generics make it impossible to enqueue an Invoice through the orders queue - the receiver needs no instanceof check. BlockingQueue is still the right choice when the consumer is a plain thread and you want the simple, well-understood API; where backpressure must not occupy a thread, an async path (CompletableFuture chains, Reactor) replaces it with a different primitive rather than a bigger queue. For middleware, Jakarta Messaging expresses the pattern directly: a queue (point-to-point) or topic (publish-subscribe) per message type, with each MessageListener bound to exactly one destination so its converter owns the type, and Spring Integration's MessageChannel is the same idea at framework level - one channel bean per message type with typed conversion at its endpoint.
pitfalls: A bounded queue must handle InterruptedException and full-queue backpressure at the producer; ignoring the interrupt or swallowing TimeoutException turns a capacity problem into silent data loss.
put()/take() block a thread: on request-handling threads that exhausts the pool, so blocking hand-off belongs on dedicated consumer threads or must be replaced by an async primitive.

In JMS the destination name is the channel identity: publishing to a topic while the consumer listens on a queue (or vice versa, PTP vs pub-sub) loses messages without error, so the destination kind is part of the contract.

variants.name: Jakarta Messaging (JMS) queue or topic per message type
variants.idiom_name: JMS queue/topic per message type + typed MessageListener
variants.implementation_notes: The middleware realization makes the channel a broker object: one Queue (point-to-point) or Topic (publish-subscribe) per message type, with a MessageListener bound to exactly one destination so its message converter and business method own that type alone. JMS itself keeps the type outside the API - the wire message is a generic Message - so the binding lives in the destination name and in the listener's converter; that is precisely why the destination must be one per type instead of one generic destination with a type property. Spring Integration shows the in-process framework form of the same rule: one MessageChannel bean per message type, with payload conversion at the endpoint.
pitfalls: The wire message carries no type guarantee: the destination name plus the listener's converter are the whole contract, so a producer with a stale schema is only caught by validation in the listener.

Queue versus topic is part of the binding - switching a type from PTP to pub-sub (or the reverse) changes delivery semantics without touching message content, and durable subscriptions are needed to survive a subscriber being down.
